summary: An April 1st humor RFC about encapsulating IP datagrams on top of what it calls Acoustical Transmission Media, a pun on the real ATM networking technology. It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke describes sending Internet data as sound. It turns data into letters and sends them as Morse code beeps.

subtitle: An April 1st joke about sending IP datagrams as Morse-code beeps.

tldr.problem: The RFC jokingly says laptops have sound hardware but no standard for sending IP datagrams over sound.
tldr.mechanism: It encodes each datagram as four-bit chunks, maps them to letters, and sends them in Morse code using a steady tone.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st joke document proposes no recommended Internet standard; its title reuses ATM for Acoustical Transmission Media.

today: RFC 1926 is an Informational April 1st joke document, not a recommended networking standard.

sections.title: A Joke About Sound-Based Networking
sections.content:
This April 1st joke RFC proposes encapsulating IP datagrams over what it calls Acoustical Transmission Media (ATM). It says laptops could use sound waves, then presents the idea in a formal technical style.

The memo says it is informational and does not specify an Internet standard. It calls the proposal a non-recommended standard in its abstract.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is an April 1st joke about sending network data as sound. Its ATM means Acoustical Transmission Media in this proposal.

sections.title: Turning Data into Beeps
sections.content:
The sender divides an IP datagram into four-bit chunks and maps each chunk to a letter using the table in the RFC. It adds a single “b” character as a frame-start signal.

The letters are transmitted in ordinary Morse code by switching a steady tone on and off. The tone frequency acts as the sender's Acoustical Signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender changes each small piece of data into a letter, then sends the letters as Morse code. The tone's pitch identifies the chosen acoustical network.

sections.title: Frequencies and Reception
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven proposed Acoustical Signature frequencies, named “a” through “g”, from 440 Hz to 784 Hz. It assumes “a”, at 440 Hz, for normal operation and suggests different frequencies for separate Local Acoustical Networks.

Reception reverses the encoding process. The security section advises users to take precautions before trying the protocol in a crowded area.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal assigns different pitches to different local networks. A receiver reverses the steps to recover the data.
